auth.title: Get an Anonymous Name
auth.subtitle: No email. No real name. One will be assigned to you, or you can choose your own.

challenge.fairSummary: First summarize the idea fairly, then write your critique.

corePrinciple.title: Core Principle
corePrinciple.text:
Understand first.
Everything else on ThoughtDom follows from that one rule.
We built a place where disagreement has to earn its place — by proving, first, that it understood what it's disagreeing with.

existence.title: Why ThoughtDom Exists
paragraphs: Most places to disagree online reward the wrong things. They reward speed over understanding — a reaction posted in ten seconds travels further than a considered reply written in ten minutes. They reward identity over ideas — an argument gets read differently depending on who is credited with making it, which means it is rarely judged on its own terms. And they reward performance over honesty: it is often more rewarding, in the moment, to look right in front of an audience than to actually be right, or to admit you might not be.

None of this happened by accident. It happened because the platforms optimizing for it were optimizing for something else entirely — time spent, attention captured, engagement sustained. Understanding was never the goal there. At best, it was a side effect.
ThoughtDom starts from a different goal. Not attention. Not identity. Understanding — as the actual point, not something we hope shows up on its own.

principles.description: Being certain feels good. Being curious is more useful. We'd rather someone leave a conversation with a better question than a reinforced answer.

You're always welcome to disagree. But the burden is on you to show, first, that you understood what you're disagreeing with. Understanding isn't surrender — it's the price of admission to a real argument.
An idea should stand or fall on its own reasoning — not on who said it, how long they've been here, or how many people already agree with them.
We don't need to know who you are to know what you think. Your ideas don't require your identity attached to them in order to matter.
Disagreeing with an idea is not the same as attacking the person who holds it. We intend to keep that distinction clear, even when it's inconvenient.
Some of the best answers take longer than ten seconds to write. We'd rather be a place people return to for a good conversation than a place they check out of habit.
A conversation that ends with someone actually changing their mind is worth more than one that ends with someone declared the winner. We're not building a scoreboard.

steelManGate.title: The Steel-Man Gate
paragraphs: Most disagreements online skip a very basic step: proving you understood what you're disagreeing with.

It's an old idea, older than the internet. Before you criticize a position, you should be able to state it back so clearly and so fairly that the person who holds it would recognize it — and agree that you've represented it honestly. Only then have you earned the right to say why you think it's wrong. That's called steelmanning: the opposite of a strawman, which is easy to knock down because it was never real to begin with.

ThoughtDom asks for that step before a challenge can be posted. Not because disagreement is unwelcome — disagreement is, in fact, the whole point of a place built for ideas. But because disagreement without understanding usually isn't disagreement at all. It's a reaction to a caricature, aimed at a person, that happens to be wearing their argument's clothes.

This isn't a test you pass once. It's a habit the platform asks you to practice every time you want to push back. Some people will find that this slows them down. It's supposed to. The slowness isn't a flaw in the design — it's the design.

neverBecome.title: What ThoughtDom Will Never Become
neverBecome.intro: Some of what came above is as much about what we're avoiding as what we're building toward. So we want to say it plainly now, while it's easy to promise — because promises like these tend to get harder to keep as a platform grows, not easier.

items.title: An addiction machine.
items.description: We're not going to design ThoughtDom to be hard to put down. If you finish reading something here and close the app, that's a fine outcome. That was never supposed to be a failure state.

items.title: A follower-count competition.
items.description: We don't think a person's ideas should be weighed by how many people already follow them, so we're not going to build the mechanics that make that comparison feel important.

items.title: A place where popularity outweighs ideas.
items.description: A quiet, well-reasoned point should be able to stand next to a popular one and be judged on its own terms — not buried beneath it by default.

items.title: A platform that rewards outrage for engagement.
items.description: If being provocative ever becomes the fastest way to be seen here, that's a failure in the design, and it will need to be fixed — not left in place because it's working.

items.title: A surveillance-driven advertising platform.
items.description: We don't think a place built around honest conversation should also be quietly building a profile of everyone having one. Those two things don't coexist well, so we're not going to try to make them.

vision.title: Our Vision
paragraphs: We are not trying to become the biggest place to talk on the internet. We don't think that's the same goal as becoming one of the best.

Our measure of success isn't time spent, or accounts created, or how often people open the app. It's simpler, and harder to fake: did a conversation here help two people understand each other a little better than they did before it started? That's the only metric we actually care about. Everything else is a means, or a distraction.

If ThoughtDom is still around in ten years, we'd rather it be small and trusted than large and hollow — the place people point to and say “that's where I actually understood the other side of something,” rather than the place with the most users. That's a slower way to build something. We think it's the only way to build something worth keeping.
The internet has enough places to be heard. We built one more place to be understood.
